paid:2023-1.memo: The paid factor of 1.264 sits well above the 1.170 norm, but the notes show it is mostly timing. Twenty-six files were settled under the 2025 fast-track programme at their case reserve, roughly a year earlier than the historical pattern. Reported losses barely move, closed counts and the disposal rate jump, and the paid-to-reported ratio rises, which agrees with a settlement speed-up rather than a severity change. Eleven files also carry inflation language (demands anchored to recent verdicts, repair rates up), a smaller but recurring signal. Carry about 1.200: strip the timing effect, keep the inflation. The paid development pattern should be revised to reflect the faster programme rather than treated as a one-off.

paid:2022-2.memo: The 1.239 factor against a 1.079 norm is a severity change: paid and reported move together and counts are flat. One file carries a verdict well above limits, which explains only a fifth of the excess. The other fifteen files with non-routine notes describe medical specials above the priced fee schedule, repair rates up around 18%, surgical facility fees up a quarter, and plaintiff demands anchored to recent state verdicts. That is systemic inflation across ordinary claims, and the same language appears in adjacent accident years. Carry about 1.234: strip the single verdict, keep the inflation, and expect the same signal in other open years.

paid:2021-3.memo: The paid factor of 1.026 is on its norm and every cross-triangle signal is flat, so the triangles alone give no reason to open this cell. The notes do. Seven open files record medical, repair and wage costs well above what was priced, which is the same inflation seen in AY 2022 and AY 2023, and it is cancelled almost exactly by a single large subrogation recovery that the adjuster says will not repeat. Net movement is nil; gross movement is about 25%. Carry about 1.154: remove the recovery and keep the inflation. Carrying the observed 1.026 would understate this year and mislead the selection for later ones.

incurred:2020-4.memo: Reported losses rose 10% against a flat norm while paid did not move, and the paid-to-reported ratio fell. The three non-routine notes all cite the 2025 reserve adequacy initiative: case reserves were raised to full expected value with no new information on the claims. This is a change of reserving basis, not of expected cost, and the same language appears in AY 2024 in the same calendar year. Do not carry the 1.100 factor; reserves set on the new basis will develop less than history suggests. Restate historical case reserves to the current adequacy level before selecting reported factors, or rely on the paid method for this period.

incurred:2024-0.memo: The 12-to-24 month reported factor is above norm with paid in line, and 25 of the 54 active files carry notes from the 2025 reserve adequacy review: reserves raised to the upper end of the range, defence-cost and litigation contingencies added, claim facts unchanged. Together with the same notes in AY 2020 this confirms a calendar-year change in case-reserve adequacy affecting every open year. The remaining notes are routine first-year handling. Carry the column norm of about 1.237 for the reported method only after a Berquist-Sherman restatement of prior-year case reserves; otherwise prefer the paid method for this immature year.

paid:2018-2.memo: The excess over the 1.091 norm is one catastrophic multi-vehicle loss paid at full policy limits. No other note in the cell shares the fact pattern, and the other 24 notes are routine handling and closures. Treat the loss separately through the large-loss load or reinsurance recovery and carry the column norm.

paid:2023-0.memo: All 62 notes in this period are routine: first notices, liability investigation, representation letters, IMEs and ordinary closures. Nothing references inflation, a settlement programme, a reserve directive, a recovery or an outsize loss. The movement above norm is concentrated in a few larger files and reads as random variation in a young, volatile column. Carry the column norm and re-check at the next valuation.
